speaker: John Ketchum
title: NextEra Energy CEO: Powering AI and Nuclear's Comeback
question: In power generation for AI data centers, why are renewables-focused developers building natural gas plants again despite solar being far cheaper?
guest: That's what the market demands today. When you look at what the needs are of a data center, they need round-the-clock generation. While storage has made a lot of advancements, we have today four-hour storage capability, which we think we could stack to get to eight hours together with our solar generation facilities as well. But it's just not enough twenty-four-seven baseload generation to be able to power these AI training models that they have out there today, and the agentic AI models as well. So you need to have that twenty-four-hour generation capability, which requires more baseload. That baseload is coming from fired generation, and it could potentially someday come from nuclear-fired generation, even though gas is probably two to three times more expensive than what you could build a solar facility for.

points.core: AI data centers require continuous round-the-clock baseload power rather than intermittent generation.
points.note: Accept: 24/7 uninterrupted load profile for AI training or agentic inference; firm baseload power requirement. Do not credit: generic statements that AI uses a lot of electricity.

points.core: Current battery storage durations remain too short to deliver 24/7 baseload power.
points.note: Accept: 4-hour to 8-hour battery storage limits even when stacked with solar; inability of current batteries to cover full 24-hour continuous load. Do not credit: generic claims that batteries are expensive or unproven.

points.core: Dispatchable gas-fired generation fills the baseload gap despite costing multiples of solar.
points.note: Accept: gas costs roughly two to three times as much to build as solar yet is required to provide firm baseload today while nuclear remains longer-term. Do not credit: claiming gas is cheaper than solar or ignoring the cost-versus-firmness tradeoff.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because AI data centers need something solar alone cannot deliver: firm, around-the-clock power at gigawatt scale, and cost per megawatt-hour is not the deciding factor. This is from my background knowledge; I did not run a search.

A data center runs at near-constant load 24/7, and hyperscalers value reliability and speed to power far more than the cheapest energy. Solar is the lowest-cost electricity when the sun shines, but covering nights and multi-day cloudy stretches requires large amounts of storage and overbuilt capacity, which raises the real cost of "firmed" solar considerably. Batteries typically cover about four hours, not days.

So developers like NextEra, which has partnered with GE Vernova on gigawatts of new gas, are adding gas as the dispatchable complement to their renewables and storage. Customers are asking for it and willing to pay premium prices under long-term contracts.

Other factors push the same way. Grid interconnection queues are long, which favors on-site or co-located generation that can run independently. US policy has also shifted, with wind and solar tax credits phasing out and a more gas-friendly federal stance.

Solar and storage are still being built in record amounts; gas fills the reliability gap.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Renewables-focused developers are turning back to natural gas because AI data centers prioritize uninterrupted, rapid power delivery over the lowest cost per megawatt-hour. Massive AI clusters require continuous, round-the-clock electricity with near-zero downtime, whereas solar is intermittent. Pairing solar with four-hour batteries economically covers roughly 80% of a data center's demand, but bridging multi-day cloudy stretches with solar and storage alone requires prohibitively expensive overbuilding and vast land area.

At the same time, multi-year grid interconnection queues and transmission bottlenecks delay both utility-scale solar farms and grid hookups for gigawatt-scale campuses. Compact, on-site gas plants built near existing pipelines let developers bypass congested grids and bring facilities online years faster—a decisive advantage for tech companies willing to pay a steep power premium for speed to market. Consequently, clean-energy developers like NextEra increasingly pair cheap solar and batteries with natural gas turbines, using renewables to supply most hours while relying on gas to guarantee firm baseload reliability until clean alternatives like nuclear or enhanced geothermal can scale.

noweb.answer:
While solar generates far cheaper electricity when the sun shines, AI data centers require massive, uninterrupted 24/7 power to keep multibillion-dollar GPU clusters running continuously. Because solar is intermittent, supplying round-the-clock power with renewables alone requires vast overbuilding and expensive multi-day battery storage to bridge nights, cloud cover, and winter lulls—pushing total system costs and land requirements well past natural gas.

Grid bottlenecks and speed to market are equally decisive. Multi-year interconnection queues and transmission shortages stall remote solar projects, whereas compact, behind-the-meter gas plants can tap existing pipelines to deliver gigawatt-scale power much faster. For AI companies, construction delays cost far more than higher electricity bills, making immediate, dispatchable generation paramount. Consequently, renewables developers are increasingly building gas plants alongside solar and batteries to "firm" output during shortfalls—providing the guaranteed reliability and rapid deployment data centers demand while keeping blended costs and emissions lower than standalone gas.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Renewables-focused developers are building gas plants because data centers buy firm, around-the-clock power, not the cheapest megawatt-hour. Solar plus batteries is often the lowest-cost energy per unit generated, but solar runs at only about 20–30% capacity factor. An AI campus draws a near-constant load all day, every day. Covering that with solar alone would mean massive overbuilding and many hours of storage, plus a backup for cloudy weeks and winter. That raises the true cost of delivered power and still leaves reliability gaps.

Speed matters even more than price. Grid interconnection queues can take five years or longer, and hyperscalers want power within 18–36 months. Gas plants, often built on-site or "behind the meter," can bypass those queues and come online quickly. They also take up much less land.

So developers like NextEra and Intersect Power are building hybrids. Solar and batteries supply cheap energy and cut fuel use and emissions, while gas turbines provide the dependable capacity and quick timelines buyers will pay a premium for. The limits are turbine backlogs, rising equipment costs and gas price risk.

Although solar is far cheaper per megawatt-hour, AI data centers demand continuous, round-the-clock power with near-perfect reliability—something intermittent renewables cannot deliver alone. Pairing solar with batteries can cover most daily fluctuations, but building enough storage and overcapacity to guarantee uninterrupted uptime through multi-day lulls or seasonal dips becomes prohibitively expensive and requires vast amounts of land. Natural gas fills that gap by providing compact, dispatchable, 24/7 firm power.

Equally important is speed to power. Utility transmission grids are heavily congested, and interconnection queues for new solar and wind projects can stretch for years. Because gas pipelines are already widespread, developers can deploy on-site or co-located gas turbines and engines behind the meter, bypassing grid bottlenecks to get large AI campuses online much faster. For hyperscalers racing to deploy AI capacity, the financial cost of delayed compute or downtime dwarfs the higher generation cost of gas, pushing even renewables-focused developers to build gas plants as a reliable bridge or firming backbone alongside clean energy.

noweb.answer:
Although solar is the cheapest source of electricity on a per-megawatt-hour basis, AI data centers require continuous, ultra-reliable, 24/7 power that intermittent renewables cannot provide on their own. Achieving round-the-clock reliability with solar alone demands massive overbuilding of panels, land, and multi-day battery storage, which quickly erodes solar's raw cost advantage. Natural gas plants, by contrast, deliver firm, dispatchable power on demand regardless of weather or time of day.

Speed to power is equally decisive. Hyperscalers are racing to bring AI capacity online immediately, yet utility grid interconnection queues and transmission upgrades can take years, and advanced nuclear options remain years away from wide deployment. Natural gas turbines can be built much faster, often directly on-site behind the meter to bypass congested grids. For renewables-focused developers, adding gas—frequently paired with solar and batteries in hybrid setups—is a pragmatic way to firm up intermittent generation, meet strict uptime guarantees, and win surging data center contracts today.

noweb.answer:
Solar can generate cheaper electricity when the sun is shining, but AI data centers need large amounts of power around the clock. Supplying that demand with solar alone requires enough storage or other backup to cover nights, cloudy stretches, and seasonal dips. Those costs can erase solar’s price advantage for round-the-clock service.

Natural gas plants can generate on demand, so developers can use cheap solar when it’s available and run gas when it falls short. In some locations, building gas generation on-site also lets a data center open sooner than waiting for a grid connection with enough capacity. Data center operators are willing to pay for that combination of reliability and speed.

models.answer:
Solar is cheaper per kilowatt-hour when it’s generating. What AI data centers need, though, is a large amount of power available every hour, including after sunset. Batteries can shift daytime solar into the evening, but covering several cloudy days requires much more storage or another dependable source of power. And in some places, developers face years of waiting for the grid upgrades that would bring in enough electricity.

A gas plant can run on demand. Where a developer can secure turbines and a gas connection sooner than a major grid upgrade, it can bring a data center online earlier. For a computing company, the value of starting sooner and keeping expensive chips running can outweigh the higher cost of gas-fired electricity. Developers can still use solar for cheap daytime power and gas to cover the gaps.
